The Tally-class enumerator was the Bureau's census cutter: a light, quick hull built to carry a two-person enumeration team and their survey suite from colony to colony on a schedule that made no allowance for delay. Its outrigger pods once held sample lockers and a small press for registration seals. Most now hold capacitors.

Bureau Tallies fly without crews, running long circuits with the patience of a machine that has never been told to stop. In human hands they are nimble, cheap to keep, and faintly reproachful.

The Assessor-class audit cutter was the face the Domain Bureau of Colonial Assessment showed its public. The broad prow houses the assessment array, a sensor suite that can read a freighter's manifest through its hull plating, and the flanks are lined with armored document vaults that Bureau crews called "the drawers".

Assessors were built to arrive, inspect, levy and depart, and to win any argument that went beyond the levy. They mix ballistic and energy mounts with the Surcharge emitter, which turns an opponent's own weapons into a liability.

Where the Assessor assessed, the Magistrate adjudicated. These heavy cutters escorted audit circuits into colonies whose compliance was in doubt, and their arrival was itself a kind of verdict. The raised superstructure amidships, "the bench", holds a sealed hearing chamber where Bureau magistrates once heard appeals in person.

The bench is empty now. The spinal large mount, the broad shield arc and a cruiser-scale Surcharge emitter remain.

The Exchequer-class treasury vessel carried the Bureau's levies: hard currency, seized cargo, and the sealed paper ledgers the Domain insisted on for any sum large enough to tempt a forger. It is less a warship than a vault with engines, and the Bureau armed it accordingly, with heavy plate, a fortress shield, and enough mounts to make any attempt on its cargo very expensive.

Its holds are vast. Two centuries after the Collapse, most of them still contain exactly what they held the day the Gates went dark, itemized and countersigned.

The flagship of the Persean office's Inspector-General, built to carry the Bureau's internal-affairs authority to any office or vessel suspected of irregularity. The black-lacquered hull and gilt fittings were meant to be recognized at a distance and dreaded up close. The forward "gavel" houses a spinal energy mount and the Summary Judgment array.

Only one was ever assigned to the Persean Sector. Bureau records list its commander as "in residence" and decline to elaborate.

A low-power emitter that tags its target with a Bureau writ of seizure, a cryptographic claim broadcast straight into the target's own systems. The beam itself does little damage. What matters is what happens afterward: a vessel that dies under a writ has been lawfully seized, and its emergency systems shut down in an orderly fashion that leaves the hull fit for recovery.

Nobody in the Sector honors Bureau writs any more. The ships do anyway.

A short-range guided missile whose warhead dumps a heavy electromagnetic pulse into the nearest subsystem it can find. Bureau doctrine held that a vessel which cannot run cannot refuse a summons, and the Subpoena was designed to put that doctrine into practice.

A rapid-firing kinetic cannon whose fire-control computer learns its target. Each consecutive hit refines the solution, and the computer shifts more of each round's energy into penetration, so a sustained burst grows steadily more punishing. Bureau gunnery manuals describe the effect, apparently without irony, as compound interest.

Switching targets, or letting the target slip away for more than a moment, resets the calculation.

An energy projector that delivers a disruptive charge tuned to weapon-control circuitry. A ship struck by an Injunction finds its fire-control systems re-validating every firing command, which slows its guns and starves its beams. The effect does not stack. It does not need to.

A heavy energy cannon built to finish what the rest of an audit flotilla starts. The firing solution reads the target's flux state, and when it finds a reactor already straining it tunes the bolt to exploit the instability. Against a ship with reserves to spare it is merely a large gun. Against a ship that has overextended itself, it collects in full.

Broadcasts a Bureau surcharge notice into every hostile fire-control system in range. The affected systems dutifully add the surcharge to every operation, so their weapons cost more flux to fire and their shields bleed more flux under fire.

The Tallyhouse is the Persean regional office of the Domain Bureau of Colonial Assessment: a cruciform administrative station, four archive wings around a central assessment array, still wearing the ivory-and-jade livery of the Domain civil service. Every surface is labeled. Every corridor is lit. Nothing is out of place.

There are no people aboard. The docking authority, the customs office and the quartermaster are all the Registrar of Assize, an administrative intelligence that conducts its business with an unfailing courtesy visitors tend to find more unsettling than hostility.
text3: Traffic control answers before your hail finishes, in a calm, unhurried voice that recites your vessel's registration history, notes that every entry has lapsed, and assigns you a berth anyway.

text1: A Bureau courier relay: a long transmission mast with tiers of phased-array panels, built to fire compressed census returns into the Gate network for delivery to Domain Central. Several panels have been cut away by salvagers, and the rest are dark. The reactor housing at its base is intact and, according to your sensors, still warm.

A small Bureau annex in a long, cold orbit at the edge of the Assize system. Its transponder is silent and two of its compartments are open to vacuum. The registry plate on its flank, under a crust of micrometeorite scarring, reads: UNDELIVERABLE CORRESPONDENCE - PERSEAN OFFICE - HOLD PENDING ADDRESS VERIFICATION.

A scorched, airless rock in a tight orbit around Assize. Bureau survey markers still stand on its surface in neat rows, logging temperature, radiation and seismic data to a station that files every reading and has never once been asked for any of it.

A banded gas giant the color of old paper. The Bureau named it Abeyance, the legal term for something held in suspension until a rightful claimant appears, and placed its regional office in orbit around it. Whether the name was chosen before or after the Collapse is not recorded.

A frozen world at the edge of Assize's light, its surface a crust of nitrogen ice over a rocky core. Bureau charts list it as reserved for a colony charter that was approved, funded and scheduled for settlement in the year the Gates failed.

A dark, tidally locked world circling a dim red star, its day side baked and its night side frozen. Nothing grows here. The Bureau built its courier relay in this system precisely because nothing ever would.

The Domain Bureau of Colonial Assessment was the civil agency responsible for counting the Domain's colonies, assessing their tithes and keeping the registry of every chartered vessel. When the Gates failed, its Persean office at the Tallyhouse was placed in statutory dormancy pending the restoration of contact or the expiry of the dormancy period, whichever came first.

The dormancy period has expired. The Assessment Bureau is now conducting the Grand Audit of the Persean Sector with automated cutters, administrative intelligences and a complete set of pre-Collapse records. It does not recognize any polity formed after the Collapse, it does not accept that the Domain has fallen, and it is very polite about both.
